document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to the initial and reply comments re FERC's 02/20/2025 Show Cause Order
document.filer: Public Service Electric and Gas Company

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Interconnection, LLC et al. 
 
) 
) 
Docket Nos. EL25-49 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating 
Facilities 
) 
) 
AD24-11 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
v. 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
) 
) 
EL25-20 
(Consolidated) 
 
) 
 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF  
PUBLIC SERVICE ELECTRIC AND GAS COMPANY  
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 
385.212 and 213 (2025), Public Service Electric and Gas Company (“PSE&G”)1 hereby 
submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the initial and reply comments 
that have been filed in response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order issued on 
February 20, 2025 (the “Show Cause Order”).2   
In response to the Show Cause Order, a number of comments have been filed.  
Based on those comments, as well as the comments submitted in other dockets regarding 
co-located load arrangements over the past year, the Commission now has a very 
comprehensive, robust record before it upon which to establish just and reasonable rules 
 
1 PSE&G serves 2.4 million electric customers in its franchised service territory in New Jersey, 
including a number of large load customers who have onsite or Behind the Meter Generation 
(“BTMG”) to meet some or all of their power requirements. 
 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 at P 2 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”) 
(making a preliminary finding that the PJM Tariff may be “unjust and unreasonable or unduly 
discriminatory or preferential because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient 
clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions that apply to co-location arrangements.”).

2 
under the PJM Tariff governing co-located load arrangements.  As the Commission 
evaluates the issues and issues a decision, it should be guided by three key principles to 
ensure compliance with the requirements of the Federal Power Act and longstanding 
precedent and policies.   
• First, any new rules governing co-location arrangements, including those 
regarding transmission pricing, must comply with the basic ratemaking 
principle of cost causation.  This means that charges for wholesale grid 
services, if any, must reflect the customer’s actual use of the system.  For 
instance, PJM’s Show Cause filing identifies two behind the meter 
(“BTM”) co-located load options (Options 4 and 5) under which the load 
uses the transmission system to a lesser degree than other configurations; 
PJM reasonably proposes cost responsibility reflecting the actual use of the 
transmission system, consistent with cost causation.  On the other hand, a 
gross load transmission methodology that does not consider the customer’s 
actual use of the transmission system would not comport with cost 
causation principles.   
 
• Second, rules adopted by the Commission should not adversely impact 
existing customers in PJM who have BMTG and who have long relied 
upon the netting provisions under the PJM Tariff for purposes of paying 
wholesale grid services (as set forth in Option 3 in PJM’s Show Cause 
filing).  Here, there is no material distinction between BTMG and BTM 
load arrangements as both configurations result in a reduced use or impact 
on the power grid in the same way, and should be allowed to net their co-
located generation against their load in a comparable manner; any disparate 
treatment of similarly-situated customers would be unjustified and unduly 
discriminatory under the Federal Power Act; and  
 
• Third, in recognition of the vital importance of data centers to the United 
States, the Commission should endeavor to remove barriers and provide 
regulatory flexibility for customers to select the configuration that best 
suits their circumstances. 
 
Now is the time for the Commission to act and provide needed certainty to the 
industry – including data center developers, utilities, generation owners, existing 
customers and other relevant stakeholders. The lack of clarity and certainty over the past 
year has had a chilling effect on data center development, and we respectfully urge the 
Commission to act in a timely manner to establish new rules on co-location.

3 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
While Rule 213 of the Commission’s Practice and Procedure does not provide for 
answers to answers, the Commission permits such pleadings where, as here, the 
information provided will facilitate the Commission’s decision-making process and aid in 
the resolution of issues.3  There is good cause for the Commission to accept this Answer 
because it will clarify certain issues and assist the Commission with its decision-making.   
II. 
ANSWER 
  In response to the Show Cause Order, over fifty sets of comments presenting a 
wide range of views and positions have been filed with the Commission.  Most parties 
agreed with the Commission’s preliminary finding that there is a gap in the PJM Tariff 
governing co-located loads and urged the Commission to expeditiously establish rules 
governing co-location arrangements.  PJM, while maintaining that the Tariff remains just 
and reasonable, acknowledges that “clarifications” to the PJM Tariff may be warranted, 
and has identified eight options for the interconnection of large co-located load.  And as 
relevant to this proceeding, PJM has proposed that the “participants involved in the co-
location arrangement should pay the costs of any grid services they consume,” including a 
reduced level of charges for certain configurations that result in a lesser use of the 
transmission system.  On the other hand, certain parties, continue to argue that the existing 
PJM Tariff is just and reasonable, no revisions are needed, and all co-location 
arrangements (regardless of the physical configuration used) should be required to take 
 
3 See, e.g., Green Island Power Auth. & Albany Eng’g Corp., 168 FERC ¶ 61,033 at P 37 (2019); 
Carolina Power & Light Co., 97 FERC ¶ 61,048 at 61,278 (2001) (finding good cause to waive 
Rule 214 when a pleading helped to ensure a complete and accurate record).

4 
network transmission service (or point-to-point transmission service) and pay wholesale 
grid charges based a gross load basis.4  As the Commission evaluates the various 
arguments presented and make rulings in this proceeding, PSE&G respectfully urges the 
Commission to keep several key principles in mind, as discussed below.   
A. 
Any Transmission Pricing Rules Governing Co-Location 
Arrangements Must Comply With Well-Established Cost Causation 
Principles.  
A bedrock ratemaking principle that the Commission and the courts have 
articulated and applied under the Federal Power Act over a number of decades is that 
“rates and charges must reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer 
who must pay for them,”5 and that costs must be allocated in a manner that is “roughly 
commensurate” with benefits that entity receives.6  This is such a core ratemaking 
principle that is well understood and accepted such that the Court of Appeals for the 
Seventh Circuit has characterized it as really an “unremarkable principle.”  In a 2009 
decision, the Seventh Circuit instructed that under this cost causation principle, “FERC is 
not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of  utilities to pay for 
facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation 
 
4 These parties take this position even though the Commission is looking to establish transmission 
pricing rules under which the imposition of charges is commensurate with the use of the transmission 
system, as required by cost causation.  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission stated that 
“different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the transmission system in 
different ways” and any charges must be consistent with cost causation principles as well the 
Commission’s recent actions in other related proceedings.  See also Atlantic City Electric Co, et al., 
190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025) (rejecting Section 205 filings proposing that all co-located load 
arrangements pay full network transmission service and ancillary services on a gross load basis). 
 
5 KN Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 968 F.2d 1295, 1300 (D.C. Cir. 1992). 
 
6 Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009) (“2009 ICC Decision”) (emphasis 
added).

5 
to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.”7  According to the court, compliance 
with cost causation is a simple exercise –i.e., comparing of the “costs assessed against a 
party to the burdens imposed  or benefits drawn by that the party.”8  And the court warned 
that a “claim of generalized system benefits” is not enough to justify the imposition of 
charges upon a market participant.9 
Adherence to cost causation is clearly on the Commission’s mind in this 
proceeding.  Throughout the Show Cause Order, the Commission repeatedly emphasized 
the importance of compliance with cost causation principles in establishing what 
wholesale grid charges, if any, should be imposed on co-location arrangements.  For 
instance, the Commission stated that “the record demonstrates that different co-location 
arrangements are likely to use or benefit from the transmission system in different ways 
depending on how they are configured and, moreover, that those different configurations 
will themselves likely have different impacts on the transmission system.”10  This 
observation indicates that the Commission is looking for a calibrated and reasonable 
transmission pricing methodology for the allocation of costs to co-located load based on 
its actual level of usage or benefits.     
To date, none of the comments submitted in this proceeding warrant a change to 
the Commission’s preliminary finding that co-located load should pay for the grid services 
 
7 2009 ICC Decision, 576 F.3d at 476 (emphasis added). 
 
8 2009 ICC Decision, 576 F.3d at 476 (citing Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 
F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004). 
 
9 Id. (emphasis added). 
 
10 Order at P 76.

6 
that it uses or from which it benefits.  PJM’s March 24, 2025 filing identifies eight 
options; for each option, PJM proposes varying levels of charges for transmission and/or 
ancillary services depending upon the use of the grid.  Specifically, PJM’s filing proposes 
two BTM/co-location load arrangements: (i) Option 4 (co-located load with connection to 
the grid with protections to avoid delivery of system energy to serve the load); and (ii) 
Option 5 (co-located load with connection to the grid with protections to avoid delivery of 
system energy to serve the load or receive back-up service from PJM with permission).  
For both options, because the load would not be designated as Network Load (and if there 
is no withdrawal of energy during coincident peak), PJM proposes that “traditional NTS 
charges” would not apply but that certain ancillary services should apply.11  This appears 
to be a reasonable approach to assess charges based on the load’s actual use of the system.  
Similarly, Option 3 (BTMG with netting) appropriately recognizes the load’s actual use of 
the transmission system and assesses charges based on netting.  
In this proceeding, to resolve the principal controversy pending before the 
Commission over the past year, the Commission needs only to apply what the Seventh 
Circuit characterized as the “unremarkable principle” of cost causation; this means that 
any transmission pricing methodology must reflect the customer’s actual use of the 
transmission system and allocate costs based on the customer’s usage to ensure that each 
customer pays for the costs it imposes on the system.  This is the same netting principle 
that the Commission approved for BTMG arrangements under the PJM Tariff more than 
 
11 See PJM’s March 24, 2025 Filing, Exhibit A, New Option 4 and New Option 5 (Options for 
Service to Large Loads).

7 
twenty years ago.12  By contrast, it is clear that a transmission pricing methodology that is 
based the customer’s gross load without any consideration for actual use of the 
transmission system would be unjust and unreasonable and violative of cost causation 
principles.  
B. 
The Commission Should Ensure That Any Ruling Should Not Adversely 
Impact BTMG Customers, And Any Disparate Treatment of BTM Load 
Would Be Unjustified and Unduly Discriminatory. 
As PSE&G explained in its initial comments, there are a number of customers in 
PSE&G’s service territory and across the PJM region that have BTMG to meet a portion 
or all of their power needs, including universities, industrial customers, pharmaceutical 
companies and rooftop solar customers.13  Under the PJM Tariff, those customers are 
allowed to net their BTMG against their Network Load for purposes of paying 
transmission and other charges.  In approving these BTMG provisions, the Commission 
applied cost causation principles by recognizing that BTMG customers use the PJM grid 
to a lesser degree and should be responsible for paying transmission charges based on 
their actual or net use of the system.14  Importantly, the Commission explained that the 
 
12 In approving the BTMG provisions in the PJM Tariff, the Commission found emphasized that 
the BTMG tariff provisions would “encourage qualifying entities with behind the meter generation 
to reduce their use of the PJM transmission system” and would allocate costs based on the 
customer’s “actual use of the PJM’s system . .  .” and this is “consistent with the principle of 
cost causation.”  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC 61,113 at P 17 (emphasis added). 
 
13 See PSE&G’s March 24, 2025 Show Cause Response at 2, 18.  
14 See PJM Tariff, 34.22 and 34.33.  See also PJM Manual 14D, Appendix A at p. 179 (allowing 
BTMG customers to benefit from their reduced usage of the transmission system by “allowing 
such generation to net for the purposes of calculating transmission, capacity, ancillary services, 
and administrative fee charges.”).  To reflect that there is no use of the transmission system by 
BTMG arrangements and that customers do not need to pay transmission charges for load served 
by BTMG arrangements (either in whole or in part), the PJM Tariff specifically provides that the 
load of a network customer “does not include the load served by operating Behind the meter 
Generation.”

8 
BTMG provisions in the PJM Tariff (and the netting approach) would encourage loads to 
reduce their use of the PJM transmission system and consequently the need for new 
transmission facilities.  The Commission’s longstanding policy is to encourage BTMG co-
location arrangements to reduce use of the transmission system and the need for new 
transmission facilities to be constructed.  This paradigm benefits all transmission 
customers.  In this proceeding, the Commission should ensure that customers who have 
BTMG or onsite generation are not negatively impacted by any new rules that the 
Commission may require.   
In addition, as relevant to this proceeding, co-located BTM load arrangements use 
the transmission system in the same way as BTMG customers.  Specifically, both 
arrangements involve load and generation co-locating at the same site.  This results in a 
similar reduced use of the transmission system and a reduced need for transmission 
upgrades.15  As such, based on the Commission’s comparability principles, both 
arrangements should be treated in the same manner and pay for transmission services 
based on their actual system usage (i.e., based on net use of the transmission system).  To 
treat BTM co-located load and BTMG differently would be improper, unjust and 
unreasonable and unduly discriminatory under the Federal Power Act.  
C. 
The Commission Should Provide Flexibility and Optionality to Support 
Future Co-Location Arrangements 
There is universal recognition of the importance of data centers to the economic 
development and national security in the United States.  Data centers are part of today’s 
 
15 See PSE&G’s March 24, 2025 Show Cause Answer at 14-16 (discussing that co-located loads 
and BTMG have similar reduced power flow or impact on transmission in the same way).

9 
modern life, and virtually everyone is using services provided by data centers.16  During 
the November 1, 2024 Technical Conference, Chairman Christie stated that the “reality” is 
that “we all live life online” and “data center load growth is just part of modern life, and 
we have to deal with it.”17  Chairman Christie added “we want to serve data centers,” and 
“data centers under the principle of universal service have a right to be served.”18 
To foster data center development and to maintain U.S. leadership in this 
transformative industry, it is paramount that the Commission take action to reduce any 
regulatory barriers within its jurisdiction that may hinder their development.19  
Importantly, the Commission should provide data centers with the flexibility and 
optionality to select a configuration that best fits their particular circumstances and needs.  
PSE&G appreciates PJM’s efforts and thoughtfulness in identifying and developing a 
menu of options that may be available to data centers (there could be more), including two 
BTM/co-location load arrangements (Option 4 and Option 5).  Importantly, for both BTM 
options, to reflect a reduced use of the grid, PJM reasonably proposes that the load pays 
 
16 Routine, everyday uses of data centers include internet searches, social media, streaming 
services, email services, and on-line shopping/e-commerce transactions.  
17 November 1, 2024 Technical Conference, Transcript at 11. 
 
18 Id. 
 
19 The Commission’s longstanding policy is to remove regulatory barriers and to promote 
customer choice and competition.  See, e.g., Participation of Distributed Energy Resource 
Aggregations in Markets Operated by Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent 
System Operators, Order No. 2222, 172 FERC ¶ 61,247 (2020) (the Commission amending its 
regulations to remove barriers to the participation of distributed energy resource aggregations in 
the capacity, energy, and ancillary service markets operated by Regional Transmission 
Organizations and Independent System Operators.”).

10 
for ancillary services, but not NITS.20  On the other hand, PSE&G does not agree with 
PJM’s view that Option 3 (Existing BTMG with netting) does not or should not apply to 
co-located load arrangements.  As discussed above, there is no meaningful distinction 
between BTMG and BTM load given that both configurations involve generation and load 
co-located and adjacent to one another, resulting in a reduced use or impact on the power 
grid in a comparable manner.21   
D. 
The Commission Should Expeditiously Complete this Proceeding and 
Establish a Concrete Time Frame for the Implementation of Final Rules 
Governing Co-Location Arrangements.  
Over the past year, there has been significant uncertainty with respect to the rules 
that would apply to co-location arrangements, with multiple dockets pending before the 
Commission.  While there have been a significant number of comments submitted 
expressing a wide range of perspectives, the key issue before the Commission comes 
down to a basic transmission ratemaking question – i.e., to what extent do co-located load 
arrangements use or benefit from the transmission system, and if so, what level of 
transmission or ancillary charges should apply?22  In the Show Cause Order, the 
 
20 See PJM’s March 24, 2025 Filing, Exhibit A, New Option 4 and New Option 5 (Options for 
Service to Large Loads). 
 
21 See November 1 Technical Conference Transcript at 14 (Commissioner Rosner stating that 
“siting generation near load reduce system costs” and the “physics” of BTMG and BTM load “are 
kind of – they kind of work the same.”). 
 
22 To resolve this issue, the Commission simply needs to apply the well-established and 
“unremarkable” principle of cost causation.  Even though certain other issues have been raised in 
this proceeding (such as reliability and resource adequacy), those issues apply equally to both co-
location and front of the meter large load additions.  For instance, at Paragraph 85 of the Show 
Cause Order, the Commission stated, “we recognized, as does PJM, that these concerns, are not 
necessarily unique to co-location arrangements and that significant load growth more generally 
may generally raise many of the same concerns.”

11 
Commission established an accelerated schedule for the submission of initial and reply 
comments, as well as a commitment to issue a decision promptly.23  The time has come 
for the Commission to act to provide clarity and guidance as the “rules of the road” with 
respect to co-location arrangements.  Here, PSE&G agrees with PJM that “[w]hat PJM 
and the industry need now is Commission guidance on a path forward based on the record 
developed in this proceeding.” 24  Accordingly, PSE&G urges the Commission to 
complete its analysis and issue an order as soon as possible. 
 
 
 
23 See Show Cause Order at P 90 (“we estimate that we would be able to issue our decision within 
approximately three months of the filing of Tariff revisions.”). 
 
24 PJM’s March 24 Answer at 4-5.

12 
III. 
CONCLUSION  
For the reasons discussed herein, the Commission should expeditiously issue a 
decision that provides timely and needed clarity with respect to co-located load rules and 
that leads to a result that is (i) consistent with cost causation principles; (ii) avoids 
harming impacting existing BTMG customers in PJM and treats BTM load in a non-
discriminatory manner; (iii) provides for regulatory flexibility and optionality to support 
data center development; and (iv) establishes a concrete schedule for the implementation 
of final co-location rules.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted,  
 
Jodi L. Moskowitz 
Vice President, Regulatory, Deputy 
General Counsel and RTO Strategy
